name: Blue eyes theory

lead: Blue eyes theory is a recurring discussion topic on looksmaxxing forums holding that light-coloured eyes, blue above all, give a face a disproportionate boost in how attractive it is perceived to be. Variants on looksmax.org add conditions: that blue eyes help most when paired with dark limbal rings, dark lashes and dark eyebrows.

The idea draws on the real distribution of eye colour, with blue eyes found in roughly 8 to 10 percent of people worldwide, and on small studies linking limbal rings to perceived attractiveness. No study has tested the theory as stated, that blue eyes alone carry outsized appeal.

paras: In practice the theory shapes how forum members critique photos and what they emphasise: contrast between iris, limbal ring, lashes and brows is discussed as the thing that makes light eyes stand out. Members who do not have light eyes talk about eye-area features they can influence, such as brow shape, lash density and tint, and sometimes coloured contact lenses.

Eye colour itself carries no health risk, but cosmetic colour contact lenses are medical devices in many countries and are associated with eye infections and irritation when poorly fitted or shared. Surgical or laser iris colour change is an unregulated area that ophthalmology bodies have warned about.

angle.text: Proponents say the eye area draws attention first and that light irises framed by dark limbal rings, lashes and brows stand out most. Members without light eyes focus on the adjustable parts of that contrast, such as brow and lash grooming and tint, and sometimes colour lenses.

lead: Blue eyes theory (also phrased as "just have blue eyes theory" and, in its regretful form, "shoulda had blue eyes theory") is a looksmaxxing-forum idea that light blue eyes confer an outsized advantage in perceived attractiveness. It is discussed as a facet of eye-area looksmaxxing: the claim is that iris colour, together with surrounding contrast, can lift an otherwise ordinary face.[1][2]

Threads on looksmax.org attach conditions to the idea. One poster holds that blue eyes work best with limbal rings and dark lashes and eyebrows, while another points out that blue eyes in general are not rare (roughly one person in six, by that poster's figure) and that it is specifically very light blue eyes that are uncommon.[1] Another thread uses the phrase to joke about a missed turning point that never arrived.[2]

Population data put blue eyes at roughly 8 to 10 percent of people worldwide, concentrated around northern and eastern Europe.[3] Genetically, eye colour is polygenic, with the OCA2 and HERC2 genes on chromosome 15 the main contributors; blue irises contain little melanin in their front layer and appear blue through light scattering rather than pigment.[3] Research on perception is limited: a preliminary study linked limbal rings to facial attractiveness, and a 2018 study found women tended to read men's limbal rings as a health cue in short-term mating contexts.[3]
infobox: Limbal rings, lash and brow contrast

paras: The core claim is that light blue eyes give a looks advantage that other features struggle to match. In the looksmax.org threads, participants add that the effect depends on contrast: limbal rings and dark lashes and brows are described as what makes a blue iris stand out, and without them the eyes are described as less striking.[1] Some posters distinguish common blue from "light" blue, saying that only the latter is rare and therefore valued.[1]
The reverse form, "shoulda had blue eyes theory," appears as a way of expressing that a different set of genetics might have changed a person's outcomes.[2]

About 8-10 percent of people worldwide have blue eyes, most commonly around the Baltic Sea and in northern and eastern Europe, with smaller numbers in southern Europe, Central and South Asia, North Africa and West Asia.[3] Among white Americans, a 2002 study found blue eyes in 33.8 percent of those born 1936-1951 versus 57.4 percent of those born 1899-1905, and Wikipedia reports that the rate has kept falling among American children.[3] This is the background to forum claims that very light blue eyes are scarce.

In 2008 a University of Copenhagen team reported that blue-eyed people share the same OCA2 region DNA sequence, suggesting a common ancestor, and proposed an origin 6,000-10,000 years ago; later ancient DNA with the variant from far older remains led to revision, and a 2020 paper proposed a Near Eastern origin around 42,000 years ago.[3] Ancient DNA from the Bronze Age Siberian steppe suggested that at least 60 percent of sampled individuals had blue or green eyes.[3]

Human eye colour is determined by several genes, with OCA2 and HERC2 the chief ones; a regulatory variant in HERC2 lowers OCA2 expression and with it melanin production in the iris.[3] Blue eyes contain no blue pigment; the colour is structural.[3] A 2008 University of Copenhagen study traced the blue-eye variant to a common ancestor, though later ancient-DNA work suggests an older origin.[3] Perceived colour also changes with lighting and surrounding hues.[3]

A limbal ring is a darkened band around the edge of the iris that arises from the optical properties of the corneal limbus and is not present in everyone.[3] Wikipedia's eye colour article says its thickness and prominence may relate to health or youthfulness and may contribute to perceived facial attractiveness, citing a 2011 preliminary study and a 2018 study on women's perceptions of men's limbal rings.[3] Forum posters treat the ring as one of the conditions that makes a blue iris stand out.[1]
No studies found testing blue eyes theory as framed by forum members. Related preliminary research on limbal rings and perceived attractiveness is summarised above.[3]

The theory sits within a wider forum habit of ranking individual features by their weight in overall appeal. Discussion tends to be brief and photo-driven, such as reactions to comments under social-media videos.[1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, blue eyes theory appears in short threads that react to social-media commentary and to personal photos.[1][2]
